# The parallelism ladder {#sec-ladder}

::: {.tldr}
Climb the ladder only as far as your problem needs: **serial → job array → multicore → MPI →
GPU**. Each rung is more powerful and more complex. Most "make it faster" problems are solved
one or two rungs up — usually by a job array.
:::

## Climb only as high as you need

MPI and GPUs sound like "real HPC," but the right answer is usually lower on the ladder and
simpler. Match the rung to the *shape* of your problem.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-ladder
%%| fig-cap: "The parallelism ladder. Climb only as high as the problem needs; most work is solved at the job-array rung (highlighted)."
flowchart LR
    A["Serial<br/>1 core"] --> B["Job array<br/>many independent runs"]
    B --> C["Multicore<br/>threads, 1 node"]
    C --> D["MPI<br/>1 program, many nodes"]
    D --> E["GPU<br/>ML / PINNs"]
    style B stroke-width:3px,stroke:#4a2c82
```

### Rung 1 — Serial

One core, one task. Fine for small jobs, and the right baseline: get it correct on one core
first. If a serial job is fast enough, you're done — don't parallelize unnecessarily.

```bash
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
```

### Rung 2 — Job array (many independent serial runs)

If you need to run the *same* thing many times over different inputs — a parameter sweep, an
ensemble, per-file processing — this is almost always the answer. Low complexity, and it
backfills well (@sec-arrays).

```bash
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20
python run.py --id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
```
### Rung 3 — Multicore (one program, many threads, one node)

If a *single* run is too slow and your code is multithreaded (OpenMP, or numpy/xarray/PyTorch
using many cores), give it more cores on one node:

```bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
./my_threaded_program
```

Only ask for as many cores as your code actually scales to — check with `seff` afterward
(@sec-resources). Doubling cores rarely doubles speed.

### Rung 4 — MPI (one program across many nodes)

When a single problem is too big for one node — a domain-decomposed simulation like WRF, where
pieces must exchange data every step — you need **MPI**: one program, many processes across
many nodes, communicating.

```bash
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=384                 # e.g. 96 tasks/node × 4 nodes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 openmpi/5.0.10
srun ./my_mpi_simulation             # srun launches the MPI ranks
```

Use `srun` (not `mpirun`) to launch — it's integrated with Slurm and gets the task layout
right automatically. MPI is a step up in complexity; use it only when a problem won't fit on
one node. For long MPI runs, prefer `non-investor` and checkpoint (@sec-preemption).

### Rung 5 — GPU

For workloads built for GPUs — deep learning, PINNs, some CFD/linear algebra — a GPU can beat
dozens of CPU cores, but only if your code actually targets the GPU (@sec-gpu); a CPU program
gains nothing from a GPU node except a longer queue. Develop on `mb-a30`, scale up to
`mb-h100` for real training (@sec-queue-times).

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=mb-a30
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
python train.py
```

## Choosing a rung

| Your situation | Rung |
|---|---|
| It's already fast enough | Serial |
| "Run this many times over different inputs" | **Job array** (start here) |
| One run is slow; code uses threads | Multicore |
| One problem too big for a single node; parts must communicate | MPI |
| Code is written for GPUs (ML/PINN) | GPU |

You can combine rungs — e.g. an **array of multicore jobs** (a sweep where each run uses 8
cores), which covers a large fraction of real research computing. Start as low as you can;
climb only when you need to.
